question: Is it better to be good, or effective?

lines.text: Is it better to be good, or to be effective? Two philosophers. You pick a side.
Good. Doing wrong damages the only thing that's really you: your soul. Better to suffer injustice than to commit it.
His claim: doing wrong hurts the doer most.
Look at how people actually live, not how they should. A man who's good in every way is ruined among so many who aren't.
His claim: in a world that isn't good, pure goodness loses.
Your prince lies, kills, breaks his word. He wins a city and loses himself.
I served Florence's republic. Good men ran it. In 1512 it fell in weeks, and the winners tortured me. Goodness without force protects nobody.
lines.say: I served Florence's republic. Good men ran it. In fifteen-twelve it fell in weeks, and the winners tortured me. Goodness without force protects nobody.

lines.text: He says power rots the soul. But a goodness that can't protect anyone isn't good enough. Point, Machiavelli.
Then I'll win the long game. Athens silenced me. Twenty-four centuries later, you're still quoting me.
So your goodness won by reputation. Results and appearances. That's my whole book.
Socrates defended goodness by what it won. That's his rival's rule. Machiavelli wins.
So take what's useful for you. Socrates gives you the line you won't cross. Machiavelli shows you how others win by crossing it. Know your line. Know the game.
Which brings you back to the question.
